Welcome to the clinic, I am Dr. Agent. Please describe in detail when you first noticed your double vision, difficulty climbing stairs, and upper limb weakness, and whether these symptoms have been getting worse over time.

To start our investigation, can you tell me if your eyes move differently when you look in different directions, and if you experience any drooping of your eyelids or slurred speech?

The blood work results indicate elevated Acetylcholine Receptor Antibodies, which points towards an autoimmune condition affecting neuromuscular transmission. Given your symptoms of double vision, weakness in your arms, and difficulty climbing stairs, does your difficulty climbing stairs feel more like your legs are weak (proximal) or like your feet are numb (distal)?

REQUEST TEST: Quantitative Sensory Nerve Conduction Study.
REQUEST IMAGES: CT Chest.

speaker: Doctor
text: The test results confirm elevated Acetylcholine Receptor Antibodies with a normal chest CT, which strongly supports a diagnosis of Myasthenia Gravis and rules out a thymoma. Since we have identified the underlying autoimmune etiology, I need to determine the specific distribution of your muscle weakness to guide treatment. Is your difficulty climbing stairs due to weakness in your thighs and hips (proximal), and does your upper limb weakness affect lifting objects against gravity or fine motor tasks like buttoning a shirt?

speaker: Patient
text: The double vision usually happens when I look up or down, and the weakness in my arms and legs gets worse after activity but improves if I rest. I have not noticed balance problems or numbness.

speaker: Doctor
text:
The worsening of your weakness with activity and improvement with rest, combined with double vision upon looking up or down, is classic for myasthenic fatigue. Since your antibodies are positive and imaging has ruled out a thymoma, I need to confirm the diagnosis with a functional test before we proceed to treatment.

DIAGNOSIS READY: Myasthenia Gravis
